project_tracker_diagnostic: Often cross-shaped leaves, but the stronger traits are thick yellowish twigs with stellate hairs and a densely harsh stellate-hairy lower leaf surface.
verified_target_counties: Hays; Travis; Bastrop; Williamson; Bell; Blanco; Burnet; Gillespie; San Saba; Frio

morphology_keys.habit: Deciduous tree of dry uplands, ridges, prairies, clays, sands, and limestone hills.
morphology_keys.twigs: Typically thick/yellowish with stellate pubescence; useful when leaf outline is atypical.
morphology_keys.leaves: Frequently cruciform/cross-shaped with broad squarish middle lobes, but shape is variable; lower surface densely harsh with stellate hairs.
morphology_keys.acorn: Cup deeply saucer-shaped and may enclose roughly one-quarter to two-thirds of the nut.
best_field_traits: Leaf blade typically 40–150 × 20–100 mm, lobes rounded or spatulate, distal two lobes often nearly perpendicular to midrib (cross shape variable).
Leaf underside includes crowded yellowish glandular hairs and scattered minute 6–8-rayed appressed/semiappressed stellate hairs; often harsh, NOT densely velvety.
Twigs usually 2–5 mm thick, densely stellate-pubescent, yellowish or grayish; terminal buds reddish brown, to 4 mm, sparsely pubescent.
Acorn cup deeply saucer-shaped, about 7–12(–18) mm deep × 10–15(–25) mm wide, tightly appressed scales, 1/4–2/3 of nut; nut 10–20 mm long.
White-oak-group acorns typically mature in the first growing season (annual), unlike blackjack oak's biennial fruit.

photo_strategy.oak_specific_tightening: Prioritize multi-photo late-summer/fall observations to increase the chance of mature leaves and acorns, plus curated taxon reference photos.

look_here_first: Check multiple mature leaf lobe tips: usually rounded with NO terminal bristle. If the leaf lacks a clear cross-shaped outline, look at thick (2–5 mm), often yellowish, densely stellate-hairy twigs and the harsh/stippled LOWER leaf surface with crowded yellowish glandular hairs plus minute stellate hairs. Confirm small reddish-brown buds (usually ≤4 mm) and scaly light-gray bark.

diagnostic_comparison.where_to_look_first: First inspect terminal lobe bristles; then terminal buds, twig pubescence, abaxial hair type and mature bark; use cups and fruit maturation when present.

pair_specific_tie_breakers.quercus-marilandica: Blackjack's 3–5 broad distal lobes bear small awns/bristles (red oak), shiny upper face, dark blocky bark, and larger tawny-hairy distinctly 5-angled terminal buds (5–10 mm). Post oak may overlap in outline but has rounded non-bristled lobe tips, stout stellate-hairy twigs and small sparsely hairy buds.
pair_specific_tie_breakers.quercus-buckleyi: Texas red oak has more deeply cut bristle-tipped lobes, frequently more pointed than post oak's rounded lobes; use bud and twig hairs if leaves atypical.

unreliable_alone: Cross-shaped leaf is common but not universal; some blackjack leaves may resemble post oak silhouette.
A leaf's 'fuzzy' appearance alone is inadequate; inspect hair types and twig width.
Habitat (dry uplands) overlaps with blackjack; separate using multiple organs.
diagnostic_comparison.hybrid_guardrail: Possible intermediates; don't force species ID from variable silhouette alone.

needs: Round non-bristled terminal lobe tip, macro with scale
Twig at node: yellowish stellate hairs and its diameter with ruler
Leaf underside 10–20×: yellowish glandular hairs + stellate hairs
Bud profile with ruler; compare ≤4 mm vs blackjack 5–10 mm
Ripe cup and nut, then mature bark
Matched same-scale adult leaves from SAME tree; do not use young water-sprout leaves as the type
